analysis.one_liner: Adds dental care coverage, including cleanings, fillings, dentures, and emergencies, to Medicare.
analysis.headline: The Medicare dental coverage bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in June 2023 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare currently excludes dental care, so seniors pay out of pocket or go without cleanings, fillings, root canals, and dentures. This bill would have added routine, basic, major, and emergency dental services and dental prostheses to Medicare, phasing in federal payment up to 80% of the standard rate and covering 80% immediately for low-income beneficiaries. It also would have made the federal government cover the full share of dental cost-sharing for low-income Medicare beneficiaries. The bill never advanced past its referral to the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 65 million people on Medicare would gain coverage for dental care they currently pay for entirely out of pocket or skip. Low-income beneficiaries would get 80% coverage immediately, and the federal government would pick up 100% of states' costs for dental cost-sharing for low-income Medicare beneficiaries.

how_it_helps.text: Medicare would cover routine diagnostic and preventive care such as cleanings, exams, and x-rays, limited to two cleanings and two exams per 12 months [S3].

The bill covers basic services like fillings and extractions, major services like root canals, crowns, and dentures, emergency dental care, and dental prostheses, which Medicare currently excludes [S2][S3].
Federal payment for dental services phases in over eight years, reaching 80% of the standard rate, but low-income beneficiaries ('subsidy eligible individuals') get the 80% rate immediately [S3].
The federal government would pay 100% of the Medicaid share of dental cost-sharing for qualified Medicare beneficiaries, relieving states of that cost [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government and Medicare's financing sources (payroll taxes and premiums) bear the cost of a new benefits program. Because the federal payment rate phases in from 0% in the first year, dentists would initially face the lowest reimbursement, which could limit participation early on.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and the Medicare program

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a new open-ended federal entitlement with no dedicated funding source in the bill text, adding to Medicare spending [S3].

The payment phase-in (0% federal payment the first year, rising 10 points annually to 80% by year eight) is far below typical private dental payment rates at the start, which could lead many dentists to not accept Medicare dental patients early in the program [S3].

Coverage carries limits and secretarial discretion: frequency limits on cleanings, exams, and prostheses (one set of dentures every five years), and authority for prior authorization and other restrictions, meaning actual coverage could be narrower than the headline benefit [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is substantial: dental disease is common in older adults, untreated oral pain and infection drive emergency room visits and worsen other conditions, and out-of-pocket dental costs are one of the largest uncovered medical expenses seniors face. The main cost is federal spending, and the design has real weaknesses, particularly the eight-year payment phase-in that would likely suppress dentist participation in the early years. The Secretary's discretion to impose limits is a hedge, but also a source of uncertainty. On balance this is a straightforward coverage expansion with conventional Medicare financing, not a badly designed bill.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat until Congress ended with no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Senator Cardin introduced the Medicare Dental Benefit Act on June 15, 2023, joined by five Democratic cosponsors [S1][S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the day it was introduced; the action history shows no further action of any kind [S5].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died in committee without ever coming to a vote in either chamber [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained a benefit from the bill dying; the status quo persisted, which is most favorable to Medicare's fiscal bottom line and to private dental insurance and dental practices, which continue to bill seniors directly. Seniors continue to pay out of pocket for dental care.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Medicare's budget and dental care's private billing status quo

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Democratic sponsors (the sponsor plus 5 of 48 Senate Democrats as cosponsors) and never came to a vote, so no roll-call shows whether the opposition was partisan; the obstruction itself was the committee's inaction.

industries.note: Medicare would become a new payer for services dentists currently bill seniors directly, expanding their patient base and revenue. The low phase-in payment rates would make early participation financially unattractive, however.

industries.industry: Private dental insurance and Medigap insurers
industries.note: A Medicare dental benefit would reduce demand for the standalone dental policies and riders insurers sell to seniors to fill exactly this gap. Their loss would be seniors' gain, since those premiums are what people pay now to cover dental care.
Many MA plans now offer limited dental extras as a marketing draw; a universal dental benefit would erase that competitive edge while raising the baseline of care their enrollees receive.
